text: Paper 3: AI Responsibility Design and Escalatory Risk
textPreview: Paper 3: AI Responsibility Design and Escalatory Risk

text: The paper studies how AI-supported decision systems reshape accountability, ownership, and risky strategic choice before outcomes occur.
textPreview: The paper studies how AI-supported decision systems reshape accountability, ownership, and risky strategic choice before outcomes occur.

text:
This is the third paper in the dissertation chain.
If Paper 1 asks how AI changes evidence-to-belief mapping, and Paper 2 asks how feedback changes reliance, Paper 3 asks what happens once a consequential action has to be owned.
The core question is not simply whether AI is present. It is whether AI system design changes who feels accountable for the final move.

text:
I want to begin with a familiar transition rather than with theory.
In more and more high-risk settings, people no longer decide alone. They see an AI analysis panel, and sometimes they also have to confirm or disclose how they used it.
That means the key shift is not only what information enters the room, but whether the final choice is still felt as fully one’s own.

text:
The literature is not empty. In fact, it is already quite rich.
But most studies focus on one piece at a time: trust in AI, delegation to another decision agent, or blame once the outcome is already known.
What is still relatively underdeveloped is the full process question: how responsibility design inside an AI-supported decision system changes risky choice before the outcome arrives.

text:
The point here is not to reject traditional theory.
Those theories are extremely useful for understanding strategic risk and escalation, but they generally treat responsibility cost as already given in the environment.
What AI support potentially changes is exactly that background condition: the accountability structure itself.

text:
This slide condenses the literature critique into one visual field.
Across management, delegation, accountability, and AI responsibility work, the common limit is that design choices inside the AI-supported process are rarely tied to risky strategic action before the outcome happens.
That is the opening for this paper.

text:
These research questions all push in the same direction.
Instead of treating AI support as a single treatment, I want to know whether responsibility design changes behavior by changing how the human actor experiences final agency.
That is why the questions move from AI support itself to ownership, felt accountability, and then back to behavior.

The broader theory does speak in terms of AI moving closer to action, but the current experiment does not claim to fully operationalize every role position at once.
Instead, it focuses on two concrete responsibility-design interventions: confirm and disclosure.

text:
This slide explains why the experimental environment is appropriate before getting lost in design detail.
Hawk-Dove is useful because escalation is not just a risk preference. It is a consequential move with external loss if both sides escalate.
The flow on the right then makes the design transparent: hold the strategic environment constant, vary the responsibility architecture inside the decision process, and observe behavior.

text:
This is the most valuable method slide in the deck.
The point is to let the committee see, in one field, how each research question maps onto a manipulation, what comparison identifies it, and what mechanism that contrast is supposed to isolate.
That is what keeps the design from collapsing into a vague 'AI versus no AI' experiment.

text:
I end by emphasizing that the contribution is not another generic claim about trust in AI.
The contribution is to identify where responsibility changes inside an AI-supported decision process, and to test whether those changes can be seen in behavior before outcomes arrive.
That is what makes Paper 3 the responsibility link in the larger dissertation architecture.
